summary:
Supply the y-coordinate (First vertex V3 (vertical axis)) and the y-coordinate (Second vertex V4 (vertical axis)) and the Ellipse standard form calculator solves for the answer. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm.

The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Ellipse standard form calculator work?
sections.html:
The Ellipse standard form calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the y-coordinate (First vertex V3 (vertical axis)) and the y-coordinate (Second vertex V4 (vertical axis)).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Ellipse standard form calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

X-coordinate=C₁
Y-coordinate=C₂
X-coordinate=-A + C₁
X-coordinate=A + C₁
B=C₂ − y-coordinate
B=-C₂ + y-coordinate

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: x-coordinate = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from a = 10 and c₁ = 10.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Ellipse standard form calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the y-coordinate (First vertex V3 (vertical axis)) and the y-coordinate (Second vertex V4 (vertical axis)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Ellipse standard form calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the y-coordinate (First vertex V3 (vertical axis)) and the y-coordinate (Second vertex V4 (vertical axis)), which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports x-coordinate = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Ellipse standard form calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
